name: Gliński's hexagonal chess
description: Władysław Gliński's 1936 game, once played by hundreds of thousands in Eastern Europe. The familiar army fights on a hexagon of three-coloured cells, with a third bishop, a ninth pawn, and pieces that move in six directions instead of four.

sections.markdown:
The board is a hexagon of 91 cells in three colours. Files run up the board from **a** to **l** (there is no **j**). Each side has a king, a queen, two rooks, two knights, **three** bishops and **nine** pawns.

- **Rooks** slide in the six directions through the sides of a cell. **Bishops** slide in the six directions through its corners, so each of a side's three bishops keeps to one colour. The **queen** does both.
- The **king** steps one cell in any of those twelve directions. There is no castling.
- The **knight** moves two cells in a straight line through cell sides, then one more at a 60° angle, jumping over anything in between.
- **Pawns** move one cell straight up their file and capture one cell forward at 60° to either side. A pawn standing on the starting cell of any pawn of its own colour may move two cells, and can then be taken *en passant*.
- A pawn that reaches the last cell of its file promotes to a queen, rook, bishop or knight.

Checkmate the enemy king to win. **A stalemate is a win for the player who causes it.** Gliński scored a stalemate ¾ to the stalemating player and ¼ to the other; the hub has no fractional results, so it counts as a win. A threefold repetition, fifty moves without a capture or pawn move, or bare kings end in a draw.
